title: Lomo Saltado-Style Flank Steak Stir-Fry with Roasted Potatoes and Rice
description: Peru's soy-and-vinegar beef stir-fry with onions, tomatoes and chile, served with oven potato wedges and rice. One pound of flank steak feeds four because the potatoes and rice carry the plate.
notes: Traditional lomo saltado uses ají amarillo, a fruity yellow Peruvian chile; a jalapeño gives similar heat, and a spoonful of ají amarillo paste stirred into the sauce is worth it if you can find it. The skillet must be very hot and the steak cooked in two batches, or it steams and turns gray. Slice the flank steak across the grain so each strip stays tender. For a gluten-free version use gluten-free tamari in place of soy sauce; the dish then contains soy but not wheat. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and keep the stir-fry, potatoes and rice for up to 3 days; the potatoes soften but still taste good. Reheat in a hot skillet until steaming, about 5 minutes.

ingredients.name: flank steak, sliced across the grain into 1/4-inch strips
russet or yukon gold potatoes, cut into 1/2-inch wedges
long grain white rice (280 g), rinsed
medium red onions, cut into thick wedges
jalapeño, seeded and cut into thin strips
ripe mixed tomatoes (plum or round), cut into wedges

instructions: Toss the steak strips with 1 tablespoon of the soy sauce, 1 tablespoon of the vinegar, the garlic, cumin and a few grinds of pepper in a bowl. Let it sit while you start the potatoes and rice, at least 15 minutes and up to 1 hour in the refrigerator.

Heat the oven to 450°F. Toss the potato wedges on a rimmed baking sheet with 2 tablespoons of the oil and 3/4 teaspoon of the salt, spread them in one layer, and roast for 30 to 35 minutes, turning once, until browned and crisp at the edges.

Meanwhile, bring the rice, water and remaining 3/4 teaspoon salt to a boil in a medium saucepan. Cover, turn the heat to low and cook for 18 minutes, then take it off the heat and let it stand, covered, for 10 minutes.

When the potatoes have about 10 minutes left, heat a 12-inch skillet or wok over high heat until a drop of water skitters across it. Add 1 tablespoon of the oil, then half of the steak in a single layer. Sear without moving for 1 minute, toss and cook 1 minute more until browned outside and just pink inside. Move it to a plate and repeat with the remaining steak, adding a little more oil if the pan looks dry.
Add the remaining oil to the skillet and stir-fry the onion wedges and jalapeño over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until the onion is charred in spots but still has some crunch.

Return the steak and its juices to the pan, add the tomato wedges, and pour in the remaining 2 tablespoons soy sauce and 1 tablespoon vinegar. Toss for about 1 minute, just until the tomatoes soften at the edges and the liquid turns into a glossy sauce.

Take the pan off the heat, fold in the roasted potatoes and most of the cilantro, and taste for pepper. Serve right away with the rice, spooning the pan juices over the top and scattering on the remaining cilantro.

title: Ají de Gallina-Style Creamy Chicken with Potatoes and Rice
description: Poached chicken thighs folded into a golden, gently spicy sauce thickened with bread and evaporated milk, the thrifty Peruvian way. Served over rice and potatoes, a pound and a half of chicken feeds six.
notes: Many Peruvian cooks add ground walnuts or pecans to the sauce and use ají amarillo paste for color and heat; this version leaves the nuts out, and adding them means the dish contains tree nuts. Turmeric gives the yellow color and jalapeños give the heat, so seed them for a milder pot. The sauce should coat a spoon thickly; loosen it with a splash of the poaching broth if it sets up too much. Day-old bread works best because it soaks evenly and blends smooth. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep for up to 4 days; reheat gently with a few spoonfuls of broth until it reaches 165°F. The sauced chicken freezes for up to 2 months, though the sauce may need whisking after thawing.

ingredients.name: stale crusty country bread, crusts removed (about 120 g)
baby yellow or gold potatoes, halved
long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed

instructions: Put the chicken thighs, broth and bay leaf in a large saucepan. Bring to a bare simmer over medium heat, then lower the heat and poach, uncovered, for 20 to 25 minutes, until the thickest piece reads 165°F. Lift the chicken onto a plate to cool and save the broth; discard the bay leaf.

While the chicken poaches, tear the bread into a bowl, pour the evaporated milk over it and let it soak for 10 minutes. Start the rice: bring the rice, water and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt to a boil in a medium saucepan, cover, cook on low for 18 minutes, then rest off the heat for 10 minutes.
Put the potatoes in a pot of cold water with a good pinch of salt, bring to a boil and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Drain and keep warm.

Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Cook the onion with a pinch of salt for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, jalapeños, turmeric and cumin and cook for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Scrape the onion mixture into a blender with the soaked bread and milk and 1 cup of the poaching broth. Blend until completely smooth, about 1 minute.

Pour the sauce back into the skillet and simmer over medium-low heat, stirring often, for 5 minutes, until it thickens enough to coat a spoon. Stir in the parmesan and the remaining salt, and add broth a few tablespoons at a time if it gets too thick.
Shred the chicken into bite-size strands, stir it into the sauce and simmer for 3 minutes to heat through. Taste for salt and pepper. Serve over the rice with the potatoes alongside.

title: Papa a la Huancaína-Style Potatoes with Feta-Chile Sauce
description: Cool boiled potatoes on lettuce under a creamy, gently spicy yellow cheese sauce, finished with hard-boiled eggs. A Peruvian classic made with feta and jalapeño from any supermarket, for well under $1 a serving.
notes: In Peru the sauce is made with queso fresco, ají amarillo and crushed saltine crackers; feta stands in for the fresh cheese and needs no crackers to thicken, which keeps the dish gluten-free. Feta is saltier than queso fresco, so taste the sauce before adding any salt. The sauce thickens as it chills; whisk in a spoonful of evaporated milk to loosen it. It also makes a good dip for vegetables or a sauce for rice. Keep the sauce, potatoes and peeled eggs covered in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and assemble just before serving. Do not leave the plated dish out for more than 2 hours.

ingredients.name: baby yellow or gold potatoes, scrubbed

instructions: Put the potatoes in a large pot, cover with cold water by an inch, and add 1 teaspoon of the salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, then simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until a knife slides into the largest one with no resistance. Drain and let them cool to room temperature.
While the potatoes cook, lower the eggs into a small pot of boiling water and simmer for 10 minutes. Move them to a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes, then peel and cut into quarters.
Heat the oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and jalapeños for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until soft but not browned. Stir in the turmeric for 30 seconds.

Scrape the onion mixture into a blender with the feta and evaporated milk. Blend until smooth and pourable, about the thickness of heavy cream. Add another tablespoon of evaporated milk if it is too thick, then taste and add the remaining salt only if it needs it.

Line a platter with the lettuce leaves. Halve or slice the cooled potatoes and arrange them on top, spoon the sauce generously over them, tuck the egg quarters around, and finish with black pepper. Serve cool or at room temperature.

title: Fattoush with Chickpeas, Toasted Pita and Sumac-Lemon Dressing
description: The Lebanese bread salad of crisp lettuce, cucumber, tomato, radish and herbs, tossed with oven-toasted pita and a tart sumac dressing. A can of chickpeas makes it a filling lunch for about $2 a bowl.
notes: Sumac is a tart, deep red spice sold in Middle Eastern shops and many supermarket spice aisles; if you cannot find it, use 1 teaspoon lemon zest in the dressing for a similar sour lift. Older pita works better than fresh because it toasts crisper. Toss the pita in at the last minute so it keeps some crunch; some soaking up the dressing is part of the dish. For a gluten-free salad use gluten-free pita or skip the bread and add more chickpeas. Store the undressed vegetables and the dressing separately in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, and keep the toasted pita in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.

ingredients.name: pita bread rounds (8-inch), split and torn into bite-size pieces
english cucumber, quartered lengthwise and sliced
ripe mixed tomatoes, cut into chunks

instructions: Heat the oven to 375°F. Toss the torn pita on a rimmed baking sheet with 2 tablespoons of the oil and a pinch of salt, spread it out, and bake for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring once, until golden and crisp all the way through. Sprinkle with 1/2 tablespoon of the sumac while warm and let cool.

In a small jar or bowl, whisk the remaining 4 tablespoons oil with the lemon juice, garlic, remaining 1 tablespoon sumac, the rest of the salt and several grinds of pepper. Let it stand for 5 minutes so the sumac colors the dressing.
In a large salad bowl, combine the lettuce, cucumber, tomatoes, radishes, scallions, chickpeas, parsley and mint.
Just before serving, pour the dressing over the salad and toss well. Add the toasted pita, toss once or twice more, and taste for salt and lemon. Serve right away.

title: Riz a Djej-Style Lebanese Spiced Chicken and Rice
description: Chicken thighs simmered into their own broth, then rice cooked in that broth with a little ground beef, allspice and cinnamon. A Lebanese family dish that turns modest ingredients into a platter for six.
notes: In Lebanon this is often finished with toasted almonds or pine nuts; scatter some on if you like, but the dish then contains tree nuts. Half a pound of ground beef is enough to season all the rice, which is how one pot feeds six. Cook the beef until no pink remains and it reaches 160°F, and simmer the chicken until it reads at least 165°F. Any leftover broth keeps for 4 days in the refrigerator or 3 months frozen and makes a good soup base. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and keep for up to 4 days; reheat with a splash of broth, covered, until steaming and 165°F in the center. Plain yogurt on the side is traditional and adds milk.

ingredients.name: long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed until the water runs clear
lemon, cut into wedges, for serving

instructions: Put the chicken thighs, water, onion, cinnamon stick, bay leaves and 1 1/2 teaspoons of the salt in a large pot. Bring to a boil over high heat, skim off the gray foam, then lower the heat and simmer gently, partly covered, for 35 to 40 minutes, until the meat is tender and well past 165°F.
Lift the chicken onto a cutting board and strain the broth through a fine-mesh strainer into a large bowl. Measure out 3 1/2 cups for the rice and save the rest.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a large saucepan over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef, 1 teaspoon of the allspice, 1/2 teaspoon of the cinnamon, the nutmeg and plenty of pepper. Cook, breaking it into small crumbles, for 5 to 6 minutes, until browned with no pink left and 160°F.

Stir the rice into the beef and cook for 2 minutes, until the grains are coated and shiny. Pour in the 3 1/2 cups broth and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt, bring to a boil, then cover, turn the heat to low and cook for 18 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and let it stand, covered, for 10 minutes.
While the rice cooks, pull the chicken off the bones in large pieces, discarding the skin and bones. Toss the meat with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon allspice and 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon.

Heat the remaining oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat and sear the chicken for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until the edges are browned. Add 1/4 cup of the saved broth and let it bubble away so the chicken stays juicy.
Fluff the rice with a fork and mound it on a platter. Top with the chicken, scatter the parsley over, and serve with lemon wedges and a small pitcher of hot broth for spooning over.

title: Loubieh-Style Green Beans Braised in Tomato and Olive Oil
description: Green beans cooked slowly with onion, garlic, tomatoes and a pinch of allspice until silky, the Lebanese way. Served warm or at room temperature, it is a side dish or a light meal with bread or rice.
equipment: large Dutch oven or deep skillet with lid
notes: These beans are meant to be soft and fully tender, not bright and crisp, so do not cut the cooking short. Flat Romano beans are traditional and work the same way; frozen cut green beans also work, added straight from the freezer with 10 minutes less cooking. The dish tastes even better the next day, once the flavors settle. Serve with pita bread or rice for a meal (pita adds wheat). Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep for up to 5 days; eat at room temperature or warm gently on the stove. It freezes for up to 3 months.

ingredients.name: green beans, trimmed and cut into 2-inch pieces
whole peeled tomatoes (28 oz), crushed by hand

instructions: Warm the olive oil in a large Dutch oven or deep skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring now and then, for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and lightly golden.
Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant. Add the green beans and stir to coat them in the oil, then cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they turn a shade darker.
Stir in the tomato paste, allspice and cinnamon and cook for 1 minute. Add the crushed tomatoes with their juice, the water, the remaining 1 teaspoon salt and several grinds of pepper.

Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the beans are completely tender and the sauce has thickened and turned a deep red. If it gets too thick before the beans are done, add a few tablespoons of water.
Taste for salt, stir in the lemon juice if using, and let the beans rest for at least 10 minutes before serving warm or at room temperature.

title: Batata Harra: Lebanese Spicy Potatoes with Garlic and Cilantro
description: Crisp roasted potato cubes tossed in sizzling garlic, cilantro, chile and lemon. A cheap, loud side dish that goes with grilled chicken, eggs, or a bowl of beans.
notes: Many Lebanese cooks deep-fry the potatoes; roasting at high heat gives a similar crisp edge with far less oil. Dry the cubes well and do not crowd the pan, or they steam instead of browning. Cook the garlic only until pale gold, because browned garlic turns bitter. Adjust the heat with more or less red pepper flakes, or add a chopped serrano with the garlic. Leftovers keep for 3 days in the refrigerator; reheat on a baking sheet at 425°F for 8 to 10 minutes to bring back the crunch.

ingredients.name: russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 3/4-inch cubes

instructions: Heat the oven to 450°F with a rack in the upper third. Rinse the potato cubes in cold water, drain, and pat them very dry with a clean towel.

Toss the potatoes on a rimmed baking sheet with 3 tablespoons of the oil, the salt and the coriander. Spread them out so no pieces touch and roast for 35 to 40 minutes, turning once halfway, until deep golden and crisp on several sides.

When the potatoes are nearly done, warm the remaining 1 tablespoon oil in a small skillet over medium-low heat. Add the garlic, red pepper flakes and cayenne and cook, stirring, for 1 to 2 minutes, until the garlic is fragrant and just turning pale gold. Stir in the cilantro and take the pan off the heat.
Tip the hot potatoes into a large bowl, scrape the garlic-cilantro oil over them, add the lemon juice and toss well. Taste for salt and serve hot.

title: Ewa Riro-Style Nigerian Stewed Black-Eyed Peas
description: Soft black-eyed peas simmered into a thick, peppery red stew of bell pepper, scotch bonnet, onion and tomato. One pound of dried beans makes six hearty bowls for about $1 each.
notes: Nigerian cooks often use honey beans (oloyin) and red palm oil, which gives a deep orange color and a mellow, slightly earthy taste; use 1/3 cup palm oil in place of the neutral oil and paprika if you can find it. Ground crayfish is a common addition and adds shellfish. Black-eyed peas do not need soaking, but older beans can take up to 20 minutes longer, so cook until they crush easily. One scotch bonnet makes a warm pot; leave it whole and remove it for mild, or blend it in for real heat. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months; reheat with a splash of water until steaming. Serve with rice, bread, or fried sweet potatoes.

ingredients.name: dried black-eyed peas (450 g), picked over and rinsed
large yellow onion, half roughly chopped and half thinly sliced
red bell peppers, seeded and roughly chopped
scotch bonnet or habanero chile, stemmed

instructions: Put the black-eyed peas and water in a large heavy pot. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then simmer partly covered for 45 to 60 minutes, until the peas are very soft and crush easily against the side of the pot. Add hot water as needed to keep them just covered. Drain, saving 1 cup of the cooking liquid.
While the peas cook, blend the chopped half of the onion, the bell peppers, the scotch bonnet and the canned tomatoes until smooth.
Dry the pot, add the oil and warm it over medium heat. Cook the sliced onion for 5 minutes, until soft. Stir in the smoked paprika and tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, until the paste darkens.
Pour in the pepper purée, add the thyme and curry powder, and simmer uncovered over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce thickens and the oil starts to pool at the edges.

Add the cooked peas, broth, salt and pepper. Simmer gently for 10 minutes, then mash about a third of the peas against the side of the pot so the stew turns thick and creamy. Loosen with the saved cooking liquid if needed.
Taste for salt and heat, then let it rest for 5 minutes before serving. The stew should be thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon.

title: Efo Riro-Style Spinach and Kale Stew with Chicken Thighs
description: A Nigerian vegetable stew of greens cooked into a rich pepper and tomato base with browned chicken thighs. Kale stretches the spinach, so a big pot for six stays cheap; serve over rice.
notes: Traditional efo riro uses African spinach (efo tete), red palm oil, fermented locust beans (iru) and often smoked fish or crayfish, which add fish or shellfish to the dish. This version keeps to supermarket ingredients; use palm oil in place of the neutral oil if you have it. Squeeze the wilted greens hard, or the stew turns watery. Make sure the chicken reaches 165°F before the greens go in. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep for up to 4 days; reheat until steaming and 165°F. The stew freezes well for up to 3 months.

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
red bell peppers, seeded and roughly chopped
scotch bonnet or habanero chile, stemmed
large yellow onion, half roughly chopped and half thinly sliced
lacinato or curly kale, stems removed, leaves chopped
long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed

instructions: Toss the chicken with 1 teaspoon of the salt, the thyme and the curry powder and set aside. Blend the bell peppers, scotch bonnet, the chopped half of the onion and the canned tomatoes until fairly smooth.
Start the rice: bring the rice, water and a pinch of salt to a boil in a medium saucepan, cover, cook on low for 18 minutes, then rest off the heat for 10 minutes.
Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, and move it to a plate. It will finish cooking in the sauce.

Lower the heat to medium, add the sliced onion and cook for 4 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste and smoked paprika for 1 minute, then pour in the pepper purée. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce is thick and the oil begins to separate at the edges.
Return the chicken and its juices to the pot with the broth. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, until the chicken reads 165°F in the thickest piece.

Meanwhile, wilt the kale and spinach in a covered pot with 1/4 cup water over medium heat, about 4 minutes, tossing once. Drain in a colander, cool briefly, and squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands.
Stir the squeezed greens into the stew with the remaining salt and some pepper, and simmer for 5 minutes, just until heated through and coated with sauce. Serve over the rice.

title: Suya-Spiced Chicken Thigh Skewers with Cabbage and Onion
description: Chicken thighs rubbed with a Nigerian-style peanut and chile spice blend, roasted hot on skewers, and served with crisp cabbage, red onion and tomato. Two pounds of thighs feed six with rice or bread.
equipment: rimmed baking sheet with wire rack
notes: This recipe contains peanuts; suya spice (yaji) is built on ground roasted peanuts, so there is no true peanut-free version, but toasted sunflower seeds ground the same way make a good nut-free rub. Street suya is usually beef grilled over charcoal; thinly sliced flank steak works on these skewers too and needs only 6 to 8 minutes. Grind the peanuts briefly, just to a coarse powder, or they turn into peanut butter. The chicken is done when it reads 165°F in the thickest piece. Extra spice blend keeps in a jar in the refrigerator for 1 month. Refrigerate leftover chicken within 2 hours and keep for up to 3 days; reheat at 375°F for 8 to 10 minutes.

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1 1/2-inch strips

instructions: Pulse the peanuts in a food processor or spice grinder in short bursts until they look like coarse sand. Stop before they turn pasty. Tip them into a bowl and stir in the smoked paprika, cayenne, garlic powder and salt. Set aside 2 tablespoons of this suya spice for serving.

Toss the chicken with the ginger and oil, then add the rest of the spice blend and press it on so every piece is coated. Let it sit for 15 minutes at room temperature, or up to 8 hours covered in the refrigerator.

Heat the oven to 450°F with a rack in the upper third. Set a wire rack on a rimmed baking sheet and oil it lightly. Thread the chicken onto the soaked skewers, leaving a little space between pieces, and lay them on the rack.

Roast for 14 to 18 minutes, turning once, until the chicken is browned at the edges and reads 165°F in the thickest piece. For more char, switch to broil for the last 2 minutes and watch closely, because the peanut coating can scorch.

Toss the cabbage with a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lime. Arrange the skewers on a platter with the cabbage, red onion and tomato slices, sprinkle with the reserved suya spice, and serve with lime wedges.
